title: Error budget policy (draft notes) — tiered SLO program (Hosted + Dedicated)
content:
Context / why this exists
- We need a single, enforced policy for what happens when a tier is “burning” or “exhausted” on error budget.
- Current state: SLOs exist in pockets, but consequences are inconsistent. We’ve had repeated customer escalations (latency spikes + 5xx + stream disconnects) during burst traffic, and Product SLAs are drifting from what we actually measure.
- Goal: make it predictable for Eng + Product + CS what “red” means, how we page, when we open incidents, and what we freeze.

Scope
- Applies to: Hosted API (shared) and Dedicated (reserved capacity).
- In-scope services for SLI accounting: API gateway, routing/control plane policy evaluation, model serving request path, and observability pipeline that computes SLIs.
- Private deployments: reference only (future).

Definitions (draft)
- SLI: a measured indicator (success rate, latency percentile, streaming reliability) for an endpoint class + region + tier.
- SLO: the target for the SLI over a rolling window (proposal: 28 days, with additional 7-day view for fast signal).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (for success-rate) or “allowed bad events” relative to SLO threshold. “Spend” is the amount of failure beyond the SLO target.
- “Burn” = consuming budget at a pace that predicts exhaustion within a defined time horizon.
- “Exhausted” = budget remaining <= 0 for the rolling window.
- “Tier” = Hosted vs Dedicated (must be attached at ingress and propagated through routing/fallback; see tier tagging plan / ADR-0142).

Policy primitives (what we want to standardize)
1) Multi-window burn-rate alerting (not static thresholds)
- Proposed burn-rate windows (placeholder; align with ADR-0143):
  - Fast burn: 5m over 1h (page) — catches sharp regressions/outages.
  - Medium burn: 30m over 6h (page during business hours; ticket otherwise) — catches sustained partial failures.
  - Slow burn: 2h over 1d (ticket + review) — catches chronic degradation.
- We should tune thresholds per SLI type (success vs latency vs streaming). For latency, we may need “bad latency budget” based on % of requests exceeding p99 threshold (or p95 for Hosted) rather than percentiles directly.

2) Required actions by budget state
- Green (healthy): budget remaining above guardrail.
  - Normal release velocity.
  - Standard alerting only.
- Yellow (burning): burn-rate alerts firing, budget projected to exhaust before end of window.
  - Mitigation required with an owner within X minutes.
  - Deployments: warn-only gate (Phase 1), then soft gate (Phase 2).
  - Traffic shaping/fallback changes allowed; high-risk rollouts require explicit approval.
- Red (exhausted): budget remaining <= 0.
  - Non-emergency release freeze for the affected tier + region + endpoint group.
  - Automatic requirement: incident declared if not already open (see incident criteria below).
  - “Stop the bleeding” priority over feature work until budget recovers or exception approved.

3) Incident criteria (draft)
- When we open an incident (in #incidents) due to SLO/budget:
  - Any “fast burn” page for Dedicated triggers incident creation immediately (Dedicated customers expect explicit comms + it tends to be account-impacting).
  - Any exhausted budget state for Dedicated triggers incident (even if no active page) unless it’s already explained by a known external event with documented exception.
  - Hosted incidents: require incident if fast burn OR if multiple regions are impacted OR if streaming disconnects spike above threshold for >30m.
- Incident roles: IC + Comms + Scribe required once we decide it’s an incident; Comms is particularly important when impact is tier-specific.

Consequences (draft; needs review from Eng + Product)
A) Release controls
- Release freeze scope: only for the affected tier and relevant components when possible.
  - Example: Dedicated EU-West exhaustion for chat/completions should freeze routing + serving changes that can impact that path in EU-West; doesn’t necessarily freeze unrelated internal tooling.
- Enforcement phases:
  - Phase 0: dashboards only (no gating) — 1 week.
  - Phase 1: warn-only gate in CI/CD when tier is burning/exhausted (log overrides, notify Slack) — 2–3 weeks.
  - Phase 2: soft gate when exhausted (approval required) — remainder of quarter.
  - Phase 3: hard gate (block non-emergency deploys when exhausted) — after alert + policy stability.

B) Operational requirements
- During active burn:
  - Assign an “Error Budget Owner” (EBO) per event — usually on-call SRE, but can be delegated to Routing/Serving if root cause is clear.
  - Required: mitigation plan posted in incident channel / SRE channel with ETA and next update time.
- After burn event (if any paging or exhaustion):
  - Blameless post-incident review required for Dedicated; for Hosted, required if it exceeded a severity threshold (TBD) or if it caused customer escalations.
  - Action items must include: fix + prevention + detection improvements, plus verification that SLI accounting is correct.

C) Product / customer-facing implications
- Need to explicitly document that internal SLOs drive operational behavior; SLAs are separate but should map.
- For Dedicated: expected to share a customer-facing summary (at least: timeline, impact, mitigations) for significant events. CS/SE needs a consistent explanation of “error budget burned” that doesn’t over-commit.

Exception criteria (draft)
We need a formal exception path to prevent the policy from blocking critical work, while not turning exceptions into the default.

Allowed exceptions (examples)
- Emergency fixes: changes that directly mitigate the active budget burn (e.g., rollback, config change to reduce errors, capacity move, routing policy update).
- Security/compliance hotfix: critical vulnerability remediation.
- External dependency events: cloud provider network incident, upstream auth/KMS outage, etc., if we can conclusively attribute impact and we have evidence.
- Measurement/telemetry failures: if SLI is wrong due to missing tags, ingest outage, or known metric bug (must be documented + fixed).

Not allowed (examples)
- Feature work / performance optimizations that are “probably safe” but not directly mitigating.
- “We need to ship for customer X” without tying to mitigation or explicitly accepting additional risk with exec sign-off.

Exception process (proposal)
- Who can approve:
  - Dedicated exhaustion: Sean Gallagher (Dir SRE) or Rafael Mendes (SRE Mgr) + the owning EM (Routing/Serving/Telemetry) depending on component.
  - Hosted exhaustion: SRE on-call can approve emergency mitigations; non-mitigating deploy exceptions require SRE leadership.
- Documentation requirements:
  - Link to the budget state dashboard + current burn-rate alert(s).
  - What change is being shipped, why it is safe, and what rollback plan exists.
  - Time-bounded: exception expires in 24h (or after the deploy) and must be referenced in the post-incident notes.
- Logging:
  - All overrides must be logged by CI gate and posted to #eng-sre (or a dedicated #release-approvals channel).

Open questions (need answers before we publish)
1) Budget windows
- Do we standardize on 28-day rolling for all tiers, with a 7-day “tracking” view? Or do we use different windows per tier (Dedicated might prefer 30-day aligned to billing month)?

2) What exactly counts against success-rate SLI?
- Counting rules we need to freeze in policy:
  - 5xx: count (obvious).
  - 429: likely excluded from “availability SLI” if we explicitly treat rate limiting as non-availability, but this is contentious for Dedicated (they expect capacity, so 429 may represent our failure).
  - 408/499 (client abort): likely excluded, but streaming disconnect classification is tricky (see below).
  - Timeouts: if server-side, counts; if client-side, exclude.
- We need consistent definitions at gateway + routing + serving so we don’t double-count retries.

3) Latency SLI formulation
- Percentiles are hard to “budget” because a handful of slow requests can move p99.
- Option A: SLO expressed as “p99 under X ms” and budget spend computed using histogram quantiles + burn-rate on “quantile breach.”
- Option B: define latency SLI as “% of requests under X ms” (preferred for budgeting, easier to reason about spend).
- We should pick one per tier/endpoint class, and keep it consistent.

4) Streaming reliability accounting
- What counts as a “stream failure” vs client abort?
  - If we close stream with error after first token: counts.
  - If client disconnects mid-stream: exclude IF we can confidently label as client abort; otherwise it will be counted and we need better instrumentation.
- Do we have enough signal today to distinguish: network blips, proxy resets, client cancellations, gateway timeouts?

5) Fallback/routing behavior and SLI attribution
- If routing falls back from model A to model B and succeeds: success should count, but should we annotate “fallback happened” and treat it as a separate degradation metric? (I think yes; it shouldn’t burn availability budget, but it may burn a separate “quality/consistency” signal.)
- If fallback increases latency but keeps success: should latency budget burn while availability stays green? (Yes.)
- Need explicit rule: tier tag must not change across fallback.

6) Dedicated per-customer vs per-tier accounting
- For enforcement (release freeze), do we freeze based on:
  - Dedicated aggregate SLO (all customers), OR
  - per-account SLO (one account in trouble)?
- My take: enforcement should key off the aggregate per-tier per-region per-endpoint (to avoid one noisy account blocking everything), but we must provide per-account dashboards + escalation playbooks.

7) Cardinality constraints
- Need to ensure budget calcs don’t blow up with {model, customer, route, region} combinations.
- Proposal: budgets computed at {tier, region, endpoint_class}; optional drill-down for top contributors uses sampled traces or capped “top N” label sets.

Example breach scenarios (to sanity-check consequences)
Scenario 1: Hosted latency regression after deploy
- Symptom: p95 and p99 spike; success rate mostly OK.
- Alerts: medium burn fires first, then fast burn if it worsens.
- Actions: rollback deploy; disable new batching config; raise headroom / reduce concurrency limit.
- Consequences: Hosted enters Yellow (burning) -> warn-only gate; if exhaustion occurs, soft freeze on serving/routing deploys until latency recovers.

Scenario 2: Dedicated EU-West elevated 5xx during burst traffic
- Symptom: 5xx at gateway or serving; customer escalates.
- Alerts: fast burn page -> incident required.
- Actions: immediate traffic shaping; re-route to backup pool; request fleet ops to add capacity; consider temporarily disabling non-essential features.
- Consequences: if exhausted -> hard freeze for Dedicated EU-West non-mitigating deploys; required customer comms and post-incident review.

Scenario 3: Streaming disconnect spike (Hosted)
- Symptom: customer reports “stream closed” / partial responses; 200s may still show up but stream events indicate failure.
- Alerts: streaming reliability burn triggers.
- Actions: check gateway timeouts, proxy resets; adjust stream keepalive; identify region-specific networking issues.
- Consequences: treat as reliability budget burn even if success-rate looks fine.

Scenario 4: Observability pipeline gap causes false burn
- Symptom: drop in reported request volume, spike in “unknown” status, burn alerts fire.
- Actions: validate metric coverage; confirm tier tags; pause enforcement while measurement is unreliable.
- Consequences: exception allowed but must create follow-up to fix instrumentation and backfill.

Draft: severity mapping (needs agreement)
- Dedicated fast burn: page SRE + Infra on-call (or Fleet) depending on symptom; always creates/links incident.
- Hosted fast burn: page SRE; if multi-region or streaming-heavy endpoints impacted, include Routing on-call.
- Medium/slow burn: ticket + daytime rotation; if crossing thresholds, escalate.

Notes / next steps
- Align with PM (Nikhil, Lauren) on which events customers will consider “SLA-impacting” vs “degradation.” We can’t have internal policy that contradicts customer messaging.
- Validate that tier tagging at ingress is stable (ENG-4922 + PR-28411); otherwise the whole policy will be noisy/wrong.
- Need concrete burn-rate thresholds and window definitions in ADR-0143; this doc should defer to the ADR once finalized.
- After we pick the final policy, we should build:
  - Runbook for mitigation steps (routing changes, capacity mitigation, rollback)
  - Incident bot automation: post burn summaries + link dashboards
  - Deploy gate behaviors (warn-only -> enforced) + override logging

Inline comments to revisit (from reviews so far)
- Rafael: “Freeze must not block mitigations; emergency path needs to be very explicit and easy.”
- Logan: “Metric quality checks must be part of budget computation, otherwise SRE will ignore alerts.”
- Lauren: “Dedicated customers will ask for the definition of excluded errors; especially 429 vs capacity.”
- Jordan: “We need a single source of truth for budget state that CI can query. Also: cache it so deploy doesn’t hang if the SLO service is down.”
